# The Whitefang Mountains · Book II, pp. 480–495
# Generated by the extractor — fix the extractor, not this file.
PAGE	480
P	The Whitefang Mountains form the northern border of the World's End, running from the <b>Huffel Peaks</b> (page 236) in the northwest, all along the <b>Great Wood</b> (page 200) and the <b>North Manmarch</b> (page 282), to the <b>Dread River</b> (page 86) and beyond in the east. Beyond them lie nothing but the <b>Frozen Wastes</b> (page 172).
P	The mountains are tall and jagged, steep and forbidding. Yet they hide almost indescribable beauty: waterfalls, deep pine forests, sweeping meadows. They also hide a surprising number of settlements. <b>Barrier Pass</b> (page 26) is closest to Stonetop, but many more lie beyond.

H2	Tor's Fist
HR
P	Almost straight north of Stonetop, this lonely mountain juts above its neighbors.
P	It's not the tallest peak in the Whitefangs, but it's tall enough. When summer storms roll up from the south and crash against the mountains, the worst of them swirl around Tor's Fist. They'll lash the peak with lightning, and in the aftermath, green and purple lights dance around the crown.
H3	What's up there?
P	Clearly Tor's Fist holds some mystery, but its nature is for you to decide. Perhaps the mountain's peak holds…
E	the tomb of <b>Stormcatcher</b> (page 332), or her son, or her lover;
E	a cleft, from which the <b>Stone</b> (page 12) itself was carved;
E	one of the last thirteen <b>Rime Lords</b> (page 316), still in stasis, protected by powerful <b>tulpas</b> (page 324);
E	a potent storm-spirit, <b>corrupted</b> by the Things Below (page 432), but bound there by ancient Rime Lord magic;
E	the domain of a powerful, temperamental <b>Fae</b> (page 94);
E	a shattered <b>portal</b> (page 306), torn open and ruined;
E	a people of great stature, who worship <b>Tor</b> (page 452);
E	the last of the <b>Tempest Lords</b> (page 398), grumpy and aloof;
E	some combination of the above; or
E	something else entirely.
H3	Chart a Course
P	To reach the summit of Tor's Fist:
C	You'll need to wait until late spring or summer to have any chance
C	First you must travel to the <b>Foothills</b> (page 144) or <b>Barrier Pass</b> (page 26)
C	From there, you must travel to the base of Tor's Fist
C	It'll take at least 5 days (from the Foothills) or 6 days (from Barrier Pass), and a corresponding amount of supplies
C	You need a knowledgeable guide or accurate map
C	You need to bring warm clothes, climbing gear, and fuel for cookfires
C	The terrain is treacherous; you risk injury
C	The way will be grueling; you risk exhausting yourselves/your resources
C	The way is perilous, filled with dangers
C	From the base of Tor's Fist, you can attempt to reach the summit
C	It'll take at least 5 days, lest you get <b>altitude sickness</b> (page 489)
C	You need to bring a skilled mountaineer
C	The climb is treacherous and grueling; you risk injury, exhaustion, or both
C	You risk drawing the attention of whatever it is that's up there
C	You must brave the final ascent: a sheer climb in heavy winds

H2	Mountain folk
HR
P	The Whitefangs host a surprising number of settlements. Most are small farming valleys, even more isolated than Stonetop. But there are also a number of fortress-monasteries, like <b>Barrier Pass</b> (page 26).
P	<b>Something interesting:</b> The mountain folk's ancestors were disciples of the <b>Rime</b> <b>Lords</b> (page 316), and Rime Lord teachings still influence the culture. But time, isolation, and competing philosophies have led to vastly different local traditions. An idea or practice that is lauded in one village might be ridiculed in the next. And in the village beyond that? It might get you killed.
P	<b>Something useful:</b> Communities occasionally trade with their nearest neighbors, and folk in one settlement are familiar with the ways of the next—at least well enough to avoid offense or violence. But if you seek a guide or informant, find one who's actually been there, lest you have your ears filled with exaggerated nonsense.
H2	Names
HR
P	Nepalese- and Tibetan-inspired: Aandha, Araayin, Bisheej, Choden, Dawa, Dhaar, Dorji, Duga, Fayurma, Hopan, Jamya, Jyat, Keshhay, Ksali, Kundari, Kunza, Lhamo, Mitis, Nobu, Nyado, Passan, Pratar, Puyari, Radhaa, Ravar, Sajadr, Sonam, Supar, Tani, Tashi, Tenzi, Tseri, Wanchu, Yonta.

Q	What drove you to leave?
Q	What behavior in Stonetop is strictly taboo where you once lived?

Q	How is (are) the language(s) of the mountain folk different from those of Stonetop?
Q	Do they worship ___ up there? If so, how is that worship different than in Stonetop?
H2	Farm valleys
P	The valleys of the Whitefangs can be surprisingly pleasant. Streams flow almost year-round, freezing over but still running throughout winter. Below the tree line, tall skinny conifers grow in abundance. Many of these vales hold steadings.
H3	Steading names

H2	Fortress-monasteries
HR
P	At least a dozen fortress-monasteries remain, scattered throughout the Whitefang Mountains. <b>Barrier Pass</b> (page 26) is one of the largest and most powerful. Each is dedicated to preserving the teachings of the <b>Rime Lords</b> (page 316)—or at least, preserving their version of them!
P	<b>Size</b> <i>hamlet</i> (~25 to 75 souls)
P	<b>Population</b> +0
P	<b>Prosperity</b> +0
B	Trade with nearby farm valleys (food, livestock, wool)
P	<b>Resources</b>
B	Tithes from nearby farm valleys
B	Terraced gardens (barley, lentils)
B	Livestock (goats, sheep, milk, meat)
B	Fine wool
B	Parchment, vellum, ink
B	Trades: bronze-smithing, weaving, dyeing, tanning, scribing, etc.
B	Rime Lord artifacts
P	<b>Defenses</b> +2
B	<b>Guardians</b> (page 33)
B	At least one <b>adept</b> (page 328)
B	One or more <b>tulpas</b> (page 324)
B	Weapons/armor of bronze, maybe <b>dark ice</b> (page 322)
B	Defensible position
P	A typical fortress-monastery has 25-50 residents, split between <b>monks</b> (page 33) and <b>guardians</b> (page 33), plus a handful of layfolk. Most receive food and material support from a nearby farm valley or two.
P	In turn, guardians patrol the region and monks (ostensibly) guide, teach, and serve as an example for villagers.
P	Place each fortress-monastery in a <b>Rime</b>
P	<b>Lord ruin</b> (page 320), and create the <b>adept</b> (page 328) who presides over the monks there. Referring to the previous page, roll or pick what their neighbors say they are, a feature for the fortress-monastery, plus up to 3 things that are true of everyone here and/or no one here. Finally, pick or roll a trait:
P	1d12 trait
HR
P	1-2 Oppresses/extorts/ignores nearby villages, rather than serving them
P	3-4 Recently lost its presiding adept; succession unclear
P	5-6 Home to multiple sects, each led by a different adept
P	7-8 Hides/protects one of the last thirteen <b>Rime Lords</b> (page 316)
P	9-10 Very small (Population -1, only ~10 to 15 souls); roll again with d8
P	11-12 Relatively large (<i>village</i>, up to ~300 residents); roll again with d8 Use the ruin's theme(s), the adept's instinct and moves, and the fortress-monastery's details to inform the philosophy of the local sect(s). Name the sect(s), mixing and matching words from the list below. A fortress-monastery is typically named after its sect or a prominent local feature.

B	Rain and sleet: pelting you, soaking you, threatening to wash you away

H3	Avalanche
P	Everyone who lives in these mountains learns to spot the signs.
P	<b>Instinct</b> to gather mass, to bury all in its path
P	• Have one cascade down a distant slope, majestic and terrifying
P	• Point out the snowpack, looming on the slopes above
P	• Note how a storm adds mass to the snowpack
P	• Point out the dimples as sun/warmth undermine its structure
P	When an avalanche starts above them, start the following:
C	A chunk of snow gives way
C	It gains mass, momentum; it'll be here in a matter of minutes
C	It rushes towards them, imminent
C	They're buried under snow and ice (d8+2 damage, <i>forceful</i>, ignores armor)
C	They're trapped, disoriented, suffering <b>hypothermia & frostbite</b> (see below)
HR
ICON	icons/danger.svg
H3	Hypothermia & frostbite
P	It gets cold in the mountains. Very, very cold.
P	• Start them shivering, despite fire/ warm clothing
P	• Test their endurance on even simple tasks
P	• Have them lose their footing/grip
P	• Inflict a debility
P	• Have frostbite set in (d6 damage, ignores armor)
P	• Have frostbite get worse (+messy)
P	• Compel them to do something foolish (go to sleep, shed clothing, etc.)
ICON	icons/danger.svg
H3	Altitude sickness
P	Dangerously thin air starts a couple thousand feet below the snowline, and gets worse the higher you go. Locals are accustomed to the thin air, but even they must be careful.
P	• Test their endurance to keep going, or just to breathe
P	• Inflict a debility
P	• Reveal that they've missed something
P	• Have them collapse, unable to continue
P	• Fill their lungs with fluid, swell their brains, have them roll for Death's Door
P	<b>Something interesting:</b> Disciples of the Rime Lords practice techniques to thrive in the thin air, but they take months or years to master.
P	<b>Something useful:</b> One can acclimate safely by ascending no more than ~1,000 feet each day, and even then, extreme exertion can be dangerous. A tea steeped from purple drakewort can alleviate symptoms, but an overdose can cause death by suffocation.
HR

P	4 Scales of ice/rock (Armor 3)
P	5 Wings (can fly)
P	6 Regenerates wounds, unless from ritually prepared weapons
P	<b>Something interesting:</b> The people of the Whitefangs fear bhoka and are well aware of the dangers they pose, but they never hunt them. They seem content to drive them off or appease them.
P	<b>Something useful:</b> The monks claim that bhoka descended from <b>Rime Lords</b> (page 316) who were corrupted by the <b>Things</b> <b>Below</b> (page 412). They cannot abide the sound of the Rime Lords' meditative chants, recoiling and fleeing from anyone who performs such a chant without faltering.

H3	Guardian
P	<i>Group</i>, <i>organized</i>, <i>hardy</i>, <i>skilled</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 10; <b>Armor</b> 2 (hides, shields)
P	<b>Damage</b> bronze or dark ice-tipped weapons 1d8 (tags by weapon)
P	<b>Instinct</b> to protect their charges
P	• Use the terrain to their advantage
P	• Take a blow meant for another
P	• Perform a feat of endurance, agility, or will (<i>reload</i>)
P	The fortress-monasteries of the Whitefangs each maintain a cadre of warriors, recruited from local farm valleys, bands of mammoth herders, or failed novices. They focus more on the arts of battle than the esoteric ways of the monks.

ICON	icons/beast.svg
H3	Ice drake
P	<i>Horde</i>, <i>small</i>, <i>cautious</i>, <i>stealthy</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 3; <b>Armor</b> 0 <b>Damage</b> claws, beak, or wing-buffet
P	d4 (<i>hand</i>)
P	<b>Special qualities</b> cold-proof, camouflaged, winged <b>Instinct</b> to spook easily and overreact
P	• Burrow/dig into snow or ice, to forage or hide
P	• Shake off a blast of clinging, freezing mist, 1d4 damage (<i>close</i>, <i>area</i>, <i>reload</i>)
P	• Scatter and flee to the skies
P	Like cranes, long-legged and long-necked, with long whipping tails. They're hardly a threat in warmer months. But in winter—when their scales and feathers grow laden with hoarfrost—shepherds watch for their sign and avoid them. Wander into their midst, and you'll get coated in a clinging, frozen mist that often leads to <b>hypothermia & frostbite</b> (page 489).
P	Ice drake fat and blood never freezes.
P	Properly rendered in a kitchen, it makes an oil used to insulate leather and wool garments. A flock of 8-12 drakes yields a ◇ jar of ice drake oil (Value 1 locally, Value 3 in the south).
PAGE	492
HR
ICON	icons/danger.svg
H3	The Howling Curse
P	Threat (<i>affliction</i>)
P	<b>Instinct</b> to make people into monsters
P	In the <b>Time of Cataclysm</b> (page 413), the voice of <b>Y'aaw'kara</b> (page 421) plunged the north into madness. Whole villages turned against each other. The survivors were reduced to marauding beasts. The <b>Rime Lords</b> (page 316) sacrificed themselves to contain the Howling Curse, but it lingers in places where cruelty and violence have caused great suffering.
P	Places tainted by the Howling Curse are <b>corrupted sites</b> (page 422), hungry places or worse, full of <b>whispers and visions</b> (see page 428) that push people towards bloodshed, cruelty, and savagery. People tainted by the Howling Curse carry such whispers and visions with them.
P	When you <b><i>give in to the bloodlust of the</i></b> <b><i>Howling Curse</i></b>, pick up to 3 options that are not yet permanent:
C	Your fingers grow long, your grip grows terribly strong (<i>grabby</i>, <i>forceful</i>)
C	You grow stringy and gaunt, and revel in pain; gain +1 armor
C	You hunch and giggle; gain +4 HP (even above your max), and your instinct becomes "Cruelty: to hurt others."
C	Your eyes turn feral; you can see in the dark, but red is the only color you see
C	Your jaw distends, you grow fangs (<i>hand</i>, <i>messy</i>), and you gain a taste for blood and raw meat
P	When the <b><i>violence comes to an end</i></b>, roll +1 for each option you have chosen. If you wrought great carnage, roll with advantage. <b>On a 10+</b>, the options you chose are permanent, and you are now tainted by the Howling Curse (if you weren't already); <b>on</b> <b>a 7-9</b>, the options you chose linger until you vent your rage on a person or thing of your choice; <b>on a 6-</b>, don't mark XP, and both the rage and the options you chose fade as you catch your breath—only nightmares will remain.
P	When all five options above are permanent, you become a <b>kyakaara</b> (next page) and cease to be a PC. Tell the GM to write you up as a monster and as a threat.
PAGE	493
HR
ICON	icons/aberration.svg
H3	Kyakaara
P	<i>Horde</i>, <i>hardy</i>, <i>organized</i>, <i>fearless</i>, <i>sadistic</i>, <i>terrifying</i>, <i>corrupted</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 10; <b>Armor</b> 1 (toughness)
P	<b>Damage</b> rending fingers/claws d4+2 w/ advantage (<i>hand</i>, <i>grabby</i>, <i>forceful</i>, <i>messy</i>,
P	1 piercing), or crude weapons d6 w/ advantage (tags by weapon)
P	<b>Special qualities</b> inured to cold, take +1d4 damage from bronze, see only in shades of red <b>Instinct</b> to delight in pain, savor fear, and indulge in every cruelty
P	• Drive their prey to panic
P	• Maim or traumatize someone
P	• Surround, harry, dogpile, drag down
P	• Drag off a captive, to eat or torture
P	These are the Howlers, the Ones-Who-Laugh, those who have succumbed to the <b>Howling Curse</b> (previous page). They are gaunt and hairy, dressed in rags, with jaws that have grown into snarling, fang-filled snouts. They pierce their own flesh. They hunch and howl and cackle.
P	During the <b>Time of Cataclysm</b> (page 413), kyakaara roamed freely; now they are thankfully rare. Treat them as a threat, beasts, with the following grim portents and impending doom.
C	They take up residence near a community and stalk likely victims
C	They kidnap locals, forcing them to commit atrocities upon each other
C	Surviving captives become kyakaara; their numbers swell
C	<b>Impending doom</b>: They overrun the community, slaughter many, corrupt the rest, then set out towards the next village

H3	Monk
P	<i>Group</i>, <i>cautious</i>, <i>disciplined</i>, <i>hardy</i>, <i>magical</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 10; <b>Armor</b> 0 <b>Damage</b> staff d8 with disadvantage (<i>close</i>)
P	<b>Special qualities</b> spirit sight; inured to hunger, cold, deprivation <b>Instinct</b> to preserve their version of the Rime Lords' teaching
P	• Demonstrate their willpower
P	• Take an extreme, unyielding position/stance/course of action
P	• Do something impossible, in line with their sect's teachings
P	Consider creating custom instincts and moves for each group of monks, based on the teachings and practices of the <b>fortress-monastery</b> and sect from which they hail (page 486).

ICON	icons/beast.svg
H3	Mountain ape
P	<i>Group</i>, <i>cautious</i>, <i>stealthy</i>, <i>hoarder</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 6; <b>Armor</b> 1 (thick fur, hide)
P	<b>Damage</b> grasping hands d8+2 (<i>reach</i>,
P	<i>close</i>, <i>grabby</i>, <i>forceful</i>)
P	<b>Special qualities</b> arboreal, cold proof, keen senses of smell and hearing <b>Instinct</b> to keep their secrets
P	• Hide in the trees or snowdrifts
P	• Try to lure/spook intruders away
P	• Reach out, snatch an intruder by surprise
P	• Crush/rend/break a grabbed foe, d8+2 damage w/advantage (<i>hand</i>, <i>forceful</i>, <i>messy</i>, 1 piercing)
P	Like orangutans but taller, more powerfully built, with thick, shaggy white hair. They dwell in small bands, in <b>Rime Lord ruins</b> (page 320) or <b>sacred sites</b> (page 362) that are far from any well-trod trails. They venture out to hunt and gather, but avoid people as much as they can.
P	Each band of mountain apes collects things:
P	a particular type of plant or flower, the bones of certain animals, bits of writing, <b>dark ice</b> (page 322), etc. They keep these hoards in a central place, hidden away, revered and treasured even more than their own children or their lives. Particularly large or well-established bands will have an alpha (<i>large</i>, <i>leader</i>, +6 HP, +1 damage) who does nothing but protect the hoard.

ICON	icons/person.svg
H3	Shantyara
P	<i>Solitary</i>, <i>emotionless</i>, <i>clever</i>, <i>stealthy</i>, <i>hardy</i>, <i>skilled</i>, <i>terrifying</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 18; <b>Armor</b> 2 (thick hides/furs, skill)
P	<b>Damage</b> orichalcum sword d10+2 w/advantage (<i>close</i>, <i>messy</i>, 2 piercing) or bronze knife d10 w/advantage (<i>hand</i>, 1 piercing)
P	<b>Special qualities</b> spirit-sight; immune to mental manipulation; inured to cold, hunger, pain, deprivation; hard to surprise
P	<b>Instinct</b> to cleanse the world of the
P	Howling Curse
P	• Stalk a suspect with perfect patience
P	• Condemn the tainted for all to hear
P	• Try to avoid bloodshed for the untainted
P	• Mercilessly cut down the condemned,
P	and any who protect them
P	• Deftly counter an attack they see coming
P	Only a handful of these "tranquil killers" remain, three or four at most. They wander the Whitefangs, hunting <b>kyakaara</b> (page 493) and anyone else corrupted by the <b>Howling Curse</b> (page 492). They are welcome in any settlement, but that welcome is often stilted, formal, fraught. Few are comfortable under a shantyara's piercing gaze.
P	Shantyara recruit apprentices from orphaned or unwanted children. Many flee from the harsh, interminable training.
P	Most of the others die from exposure or deprivation or one of the many dangers such a life entails. A rare few last long
P	enough to be useful companions (<b>HP</b> 10;
P	<b>Armor</b> 1; <b>Damage</b> d8; <b>Instinct</b> to earn their master's respect). And once or twice every generation, a master will deem an apprentice worthy, and take them to a sacred cave, and burden them with one of the shantyara's orichalcum blades.
